---
title: "Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve"
---

Allow about 60 minutes for paper problems and 40 minutes for the R task.
You need lone pairs, formal charges, `ggplot2`, and a working R Markdown report.
Use the [restart guide](../intro/r-restart.qmd) if needed.

## 1. Follow the electron pair

Draw ethanoic acid and hydroxide with the relevant lone pairs. Draw two curved
arrows to produce ethanoate and water. Label both conjugate pairs and check
the total charge on each side. Then reverse the drawing: which species would
have to act as the acid and base in the reverse reaction?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Begin one arrow on a hydroxide lone pair and end it at the acidic hydrogen.
The other arrow starts at the acid's O–H bond.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The acid is CH₃COOH and the base is OH⁻. Products are CH₃COO⁻ and H₂O.
The conjugate pairs are acid/ethanoate and water/hydroxide. Total charge is −1
on both sides. In the reverse direction water would donate H⁺ to ethanoate.
This reverse event is possible, but equilibrium strongly favours the forward
direction under the compatible aqueous pKa approximation.
:::

## 2. Explain acidity using structure

Draw ethoxide and both equivalent ethanoate resonance contributors. Which
conjugate base delocalises its negative charge over equivalent oxygen atoms?
Explain why moving a hydrogen atom would no longer be resonance. Use supplied
approximate aqueous pKa values: ethanol 16 and ethanoic acid 4.8.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Ethanoate delocalises the charge over its two oxygens; its two C–O bonds are
equivalent in the actual ion. The contributors have the same nuclei in the
same positions and differ in electron placement. A hydrogen shift changes
connectivity and describes a chemical transformation. Ethanoic acid is the
stronger acid; pKa compares equilibria, while conjugate-base stabilisation
provides the structural explanation.
:::

## 3. Predict a proton transfer

For CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂ ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺ use pKa 4.8 for the reactant acid
and 10.6 for methylammonium. Predict the favoured side and estimate the
equilibrium constant as `10^(product_acid_pKa - reactant_acid_pKa)`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The products contain the weaker acid, with larger pKa. The estimated constant
is `10^5.8`, about 630,957. This estimate requires compatible solvent and
standard-state conventions. It predicts a strongly product-favoured equilibrium,
not an irreversible reaction or an experimental reaction rate.
:::

## 4. R task: how much of the acid is ionised?

**Question:** for a monoprotic acid with supplied pKa 4.8, how does its aqueous
ionised fraction change between pH 1 and 9? This is a calculated teaching model,
not measured acid dissociation data. Use the dilute-solution approximation.

The ratio is $r=[A^-]/[HA]=10^{pH-pK_a}$, so the fraction is
$r/(1+r)=1/(1+10^{pK_a-pH})$. pH, pKa and the fraction are dimensionless.
At pH = pKa predict 0.5. At one pH unit above pKa predict 10/11.

Add the following to your report, below a sentence stating your prediction:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ionisation <- data.frame(pH = seq(1, 9, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(fraction_A_minus = 1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - pH)))
ggplot(ionisation, aes(pH, fraction_A_minus)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#176b91", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "pH", y = "Fraction present as A−") +
  theme_minimal()
1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - c(3.8, 4.8, 5.8)))
```

Knit the report. Explain why the curve rises, why its midpoint is 4.8, and why
a fraction of 0.909 does not mean each molecule is 90.9% deprotonated. Change
pKa to 6.0, predict the shift and then compare the curves. State why the plot
alone cannot predict extraction recovery into an organic solvent.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Numerical and chemical check"}
At pH 3.8, 4.8 and 5.8 the fractions are approximately 0.0909, 0.5 and 0.9091.
A larger pKa shifts the midpoint to higher pH; this weaker acid needs higher pH
to achieve the same fraction. Fractions describe a population of molecular
species. Extraction needs partition coefficients and phase volumes as well
as aqueous ionisation. The supplied curve is not a titration curve: pH is the
input, not the calculated consequence of adding a specified titrant volume.
:::

## Leave with

A checked proton-transfer mechanism, a conjugate-base comparison, and a knitted
report containing a labelled plot and your own chemical interpretation.
